description.value: The study validated a modified Empathic Accuracy Task using naturalistic autobiographical emotional videos, continuous ratings of perceived emotional intensity, and a neutral control condition to investigate cognitive and affective empathy and their neural correlates.

design.value: A staged within-participant fMRI study in which 34 healthy participants watched and continuously rated six autobiographical video clips—two happy, two sad and two neutral—followed by group-level comparisons of emotional versus neutral clips, parametric modulation by empathic accuracy, correlations with continuous emotional-intensity ratings, and an exploratory affect-sharing comparison. A separate normative sample of 60 healthy participants completed the task outside the scanner.

task_description.value: Participants watched and rated six autobiographical video clips in the scanner while continuously rating the perceived emotional intensity of the target. The clips comprised happy, sad and neutral videos.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to continuously rate the perceived emotional intensity of the target using a 9-point scale from 1, 'no emotion', to 9, 'very strong emotion'. Following each clip, they reported which emotion the target felt most strongly and which emotion they themselves felt most strongly.

description.value: A T1-weighted Magnetization Prepared Rapid Gradient Echo MPRAGE image was acquired to facilitate fMRI data registration and normalisation. The sequence used a 256 × 256 matrix, 1.2 mm slice thickness, 196 sagittal slices, 270 mm field of view and 11° flip angle.

description.value: EPI files were reoriented, slice-time corrected, realigned, and co-registered to the T1-weighted image. Structural files were segmented and used to create a common group-specific template using group-wise DARTEL registration. Functional EPI files were normalised to MNI space, resampled to 1.5 mm isotropic voxels and spatially smoothed with an 8 mm Gaussian FWHM kernel. A CSF mask time course was extracted in native space.

model_settings.value: Block design with three separate regressors for happy, sad and neutral video presentation, formed by convolution of the canonical HRF with boxcars delimiting video presentation. Seven movement parameters, additional regressors for volume-to-volume movement exceeding 1 mm, the CSF regressor and button presses as a condition of no interest were included.

Separate parameter estimates for mean response during emotional and neutral categories compared to the implicit baseline; paired t-tests identified clusters differentially activated for emotional versus neutral clips and happy versus sad clips.

model_type.value: general linear model with parametric modulation

model_settings.value: Z-EA scores for each participant and each video clip were added as parametric modulators at the first level. The nuisance regressors described for the main model were also included.
One-sample t-tests tested whether the BOLD response during emotional video clips was modulated by intra-individual variations in Z-EA scores.

Scans were split and a model was fitted to each emotional video clip in turn. Continuous participant ratings of the target's emotional intensity for each 2 s bin were entered as regressors of interest, together with the nuisance regressors described for the other analyses.
One-sample t-tests assessed whether the relationship between BOLD response and changes in emotional intensity ratings was significantly observed in any brain region across the group.

For the 20 participants who showed affect sharing in response to some but not all video clips, three block-design conditions were modelled: shared, non-shared and neutral. Separate parameter estimates for mean response during affect-shared, non-shared and neutral video presentation compared to the implicit baseline were calculated.
Paired t-tests identified clusters differentially activated when watching video clips that induced affect sharing compared to non-shared clips.
